habitats.name: Forest & Woodland
habitats.examples: Forest consists of a continuous stand of trees and includes both forested areas (generally with a closed canopy) and wooded areas (canopy more open, but see 2. Savanna).

level1.name: Boreal Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed across the high latitudes of the northern hemisphere (occurring between 50 and 60° N) in a broad belt across Eurasia and North America. Trees are predominantly coniferous (pine, fir and spruce), though a few deciduous genera are nearly ubiquitous in their distribution and are locally common (see 1.4).
Includes forest types described as taiga, coniferous, coniferous deciduous, and broadleaved deciduous.

level1.name: Subarctic Forest
level1.examples: Included for completeness sake - probably little forest occurs at these high latitudes.

level1.name: Subantarctic Forest
level1.examples: Stunted forest on subantarctic islands. Forest on Auckland and Snares Islands (to New Zealand), bosques sub-antárticos (Argentina).

level1.name: Temperate Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed in the temperate regions (under the influence of moist continental climates) of North and South America (primarily Chile), Europe, Asia (China/Korea/Japan) and Australia/New Zealand. Includes forest types described as coniferous, broadleaved evergreen, broadleaved deciduous, and mixed; also riverine and alluvial. The deciduous trees shed their leaves in the winter season. In the northern hemisphere, the coniferous (or needleleaf evergreen) component increases towards the north where the mixed forest transitions to Boreal Forest (see 1.1).
Includes Mediterranean forests but these might also be placed under 1.5 [ needs resolution ] and pine-oak forests found in Mexico and the southern US.

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Dry Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed in the subtropical/tropical regions of the Neotropics, Africa and Indo-Malesia. Typically forests that experience a dry season of several months.
Includes forest types described as deciduous, makatea, atoll/beach, palm, thorn and spiny; Florida rockland hammocks, pune rocklands, marine hammocks, shellmounds (last 4 from SE USA); bosque chaco, espinal, bosque de algarrobo/prosopis (Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay); forest in the seasonally dry inter- Andean valleys.

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Moist Lowland Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed in the subtropical/tropical regions of the Neotropics, Africa and Indo-Malesia, generally below c.1,200 m (but varying with geography and topography).
Includes (lowland/hill rain/wet/humid/moist) forest types described as evergreen or semi-evergreen or broadleaved evergreen, deciduous, dipterocarp and mixed; also riparian/riverine and gallery, Sierra maestra se Cuba, selva paranaense, bosque de quebrada, bosque sammofilo (Uruguay)

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Mangrove Forest Vegetation Above High Tide Level
level1.examples: Distributed in the subtropics and tropics, growing in sheltered estuaries and along coastlines in brackish or salt water

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Swamp Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed in the subtropics and tropics. Typically flooded for at least part of the year and dependent on this flooding for its existence.
Includes forest types described as peat swamp, bog, and varzea/igapo.

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Moist Montane Forest
level1.examples:
Distributed in the subtropical/tropical regions of the Neotropics, Africa and Indo-Malesia, generally above c.1,200 m (but varying with geography and topography).
Includes (lower and upper montane/mountain rain/wet/moist) forest types described as cloud, mossy, elfin, dwarf, Polylepis, coniferous, pine, pine-oak and evergreen, mesophyllous, yungas (to Peru/Bolivia/Argentina).

habitats.name: Savanna
habitats.examples: Savannas are transitional between grasslands and forests. They are ecosystems dominated by a grass ground cover with an overstorey of widely spaced trees and shrubs. May be referred to as savanna woodlands, savanna parklands, savanna grasslands, low tree/shrub savannas, thicket/scrub savannas. Distributed largely in Africa, Australia (mostly northern), Asia (India, SE Asia) and South America.

level1.name: Dry Savanna
level1.examples: Includes savanna types described as Eucalyptus and Acacia woodland, mopane/miombo/Brachystegia woodlands (Africa), cerrado/campos/caatinga (Brazil, Guiana), chaco seco (Argentina/Uruguay) and mulga (Australia), oak woodlands (mid- western USA)

level1.name: Moist Savanna
level1.examples: Includes savanna types described as pantanal (Brazil/Bolivia/Paraguay), chaco or chaco húmedo (Paraguay/Bolivia/Argentina), and llanos (Venezuela/Colombia).

habitats.name: Shrubland
habitats.examples: Also referred to as scrub, bushland and thicket.

level1.name: Temperate Shrubland
level1.examples: Includes semi-deserts dominated by shrubs, coastal beach shrublands

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Dry Shrubland
level1.examples: Found mainly on the lowlands. Includes (arid/semi-desert/dry) shrubland types described as succulent, thorn or thorn scrub, karoo, strandveld (South Africa), Kalahari (Botswana, Namibia, South Africa), restingas (coastal scrub in Brazil); coastal strand; xerophyllous scrub; chapparal (Mexico and SW US); enclave, matorral sammofilo, matorral seco (Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay).

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Moist Shrubland
level1.examples:
Humid/semi-humid shrubland types described as evergreen and found mainly on the lowlands
Includes vegetation on river islands and in the riparian zones; matorral húmedo (Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay)

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical High Altitude Shrubland
level1.examples:
Alpine/subalpine shrubland types around and above the tree-line in mountainous regions.
Some of the shrublands are dominated by rhododendron, juniper or birch; prepuna (Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay).

level1.name: Mediterranean-type Shrubby Vegetation
level1.examples:
Distributed in Mediterranean ecosystems of Australia, Chile, Europe/North Africa, North America (primarily California) and South Africa. Evergreen shrubs and sclerophyllous trees (low in stature with a relatively open canopy) are the dominant plant forms, and frequent fires have historically played an important role in regulating community composition and structure. The areas are characterized by warm dry summers.
Includes shrubland types described as garrigue, chaparral (California), maquis (Mediterranean), mallee or mallee scrub (Australia), matorral (Chile) and fynbos (South Africa).

habitats.name: Native Grassland
habitats.examples: Grasslands occur in regions with warm growing seasons and moderate water shortages. Native grasslands are comprised of grasses and broadleaved herbaceous plants, and are either without woody plants, or the latter are very sparsely distributed (see also 2. Savanna).

level1.name: Tundra
level1.examples: Grasslands which have developed over permafrost. Confined to the northern hemisphere where it encircles the north pole and extends south to the Boreal Forests. The area is characterized by its extremely cold desert-like conditions.

level1.name: Subantarctic Grassland
level1.examples: Tussock grassland on subantarctic islands.

level1.name: Temperate Grassland
level1.examples: Includes grassland types described as prairies (North America); steppe (Eurasia); calcareous; siliceous; edaphic; pampa or pampas (South America); pastizal patagónico, patagonia, pastizal pampeano (Argentina).

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Dry Lowland Grassland
level1.examples: Includes (arid/dry) grassland types described as hummock/tussock (Australia); estepa (Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay).

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical High Altitude Grassland
level1.examples:
Sometimes also referred to as alpine tundra. The night time temperatures are usually below freezing, but the soils are well- drained.
Includes (alpine/subalpine/highveld) grassland types described as paramos, altiplanos, puna, pastizal de altura.

level1.name: Shrub Dominated Wetlands
level1.examples: Shrub swamps, shrub-dominated freshwater marshes, shrub carr, alder thicket on inorganic soils.

level1.name: Bogs, Marshes, Swamps, Fens, Peatlands
level1.examples:
Generally over 8 ha. Also includes mires.
Bogs are peat-accumulating systems fed only by rainwater and thus have very low nutrient levels. They are usually strongly acidic, and water flow is restricted. The water table is either at or just below the surface and remains relatively constant. Fens have a predominantly peat substrate, but the peat is shallower and more decomposed than bogs. They are fed by both rain and groundwater resulting in low to moderate nutrient and acidity levels. The water table is typically just below the peat surface but there are small noticeable fluctuations. Swamps are relatively high in nutrients supplied via surface runoff and groundwater from the surrounding land. The water table is usually above some of the ground surface, but there are large, seasonal fluctuations. Marshes are characterized by large periodic fluctuations of water table or water level.

level1.name: Permanent Freshwater Lakes
level1.examples: Over 8 ha. Includes large oxbow lakes (see 13.5).

level1.name: Seasonal/Intermittent Freshwater Lakes
level1.examples: Over 8 ha. Includes floodplain lakes (see 13.5).

level1.name: Permanent Freshwater Marshes/Pools
level1.examples: Ponds (below 8 ha), marshes and swamps on inorganic soils; with emergent vegetation water-logged for at least most of the growing season.

level1.name: Seasonal/Intermittent Freshwater Marshes/Pools
level1.examples: Below 8 ha. On inorganic soils; includes sloughs, potholes, seasonally flooded meadows, sedge marshes.

level1.name: Tundra Wetlands
level1.examples: Includes tundra pools and temporary waters from snowmelt.

level1.name: Alpine Wetlands
level1.examples: Includes alpine meadows, seepages, temporary waters from snowmelt.

level1.name: Geothermal Wetlands
level1.examples: Wetlands influenced by heated geothermal water or chemistry derived from current or former geothermal activity. Often found in volcanically active areas.

level1.name: Permanent Inland Deltas
level1.examples:
Created by a river dividing into multiple branches, these usually rejoin and continue to the sea. They often occur on former lake beds. In some cases a river flowing into a flat arid area splits into channels which then evaporate as it progresses into the desert.
The Inner Niger Delta and Peace–Athabasca Delta are notable examples. The Amazon has an inland delta before the island of Marajó and the Okavango Delta is the best example of a desert inland delta .

level1.name: Permanent Saline, Brackish or Alkaline Lakes
Seasonal/Intermittent Saline, Brackish or Alkaline Lakes and Flats
Permanent Saline, Brackish or Alkaline Marshes/Pools
Seasonal/Intermittent Saline, Brackish or Alkaline Marshes/Pools
Karst and Other Subterranean Inland Aquatic Systems

habitats.name: Inland Rocky Areas
habitats.examples: Includes inland cliffs, mountain peaks, talus, feldmark.

level1.name: Dry Caves
level1.examples: Underground spaces produced naturally by the weathering of rock. Can extend deep underground, or can be much smaller rock

habitats.name: Desert
habitats.examples: Desert consists of arid landscapes with a sparse plant cover, except in depressions where water accumulates. The sandy, stony or rocky substrate contributes more to the appearance of the landscape than does the vegetation.

level1.name: Hot Desert
level1.examples: Deserts where the main form of precipitation is rain, thus would include the Arabian Desert; various Australian deserts - Great Sandy, Victoria, Simpson, Gibson and Sturt; Sahara; and the Thar in India.

level1.name: Temperate Desert
level1.examples: Not clear, but might include the Takla Makan Desert in China, and the desert areas of Turkestan and possibly the Iranian Desert

level1.name: Cold Desert
level1.examples: Deserts where the main form of precipitation is snow or fog, and thus would include the Atacama Desert (Peru and Chile), Gobi Desert (China and Mongolia), Namib Desert (Namibia and bit of South Africa), Antarctica and parts of the Arctic.

habitats.name: Marine - Neritic
habitats.examples: Submergent (below extreme low tide), nearshore, on or over the continental shelf or oceanic island shelf. [Continental shelf is the expanded perimeter of each continent, which is gently sloping and covered by relatively shallow seas (typically limited to a depth of around 200 m) or embayments. The shelf usually ends at a point of increasing slope (called the shelf break)].

level1.name: Pelagic
level1.examples: The division of the marine environment composed of all the ocean’s water; living in the water column, away from the bottom.

level1.name: Subtidal Rock and Rocky Reefs
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting predominantly of boulders (any loose rock larger than 256 mm in diameter) or consolidated rock (includes submerged coastal karst systems, but see 12.1).

level1.name: Subtidal Loose Rock/Pebble/Gravel
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting predominantly of unconsolidated cobbles (sediment size 64 to 256 mm diameter) and pebbles (sediment size 2 to 64 mm diameter).

level1.name: Subtidal Sandy
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting of loose particles of rock or mineral sediments (predominantly ranges in size from 0.0625–2.0 mm in diameter).

level1.name: Subtidal Sandy-Mud
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting predominantly of a mixture of sandy (see 9.4) and muddy (see 9.6) sediment types.

level1.name: Subtidal Muddy
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting of wet clay (any particle smaller than 0.002 mm in diameter) and silt-rich sediment (silt consists of loose particles of rock or mineral (sediment) that ranges in size from 0.002–0.0625 mm in diameter).

level1.name: Macroalgal/Kelp
level1.examples: Bottom habitat consisting predominantly of large algae, typically brown algae, which often forms dense macroalgal beds or forests.

level1.name: Coral Reef
level1.examples: Massive limestone structure built up through the cementing and depositional activities of colonial stony corals, predominantly of the order Scleractinia, and other calcareous invertebrate and algal species.

level2.examples: Coral reef habitat on the foreslope (see 9.8.3) within or around the surge channels (spur and groove formations).
The area opposite of the foreslope (see 9.8.3), also referring to the reef flat or inner part of a barrier reef or atoll.
The outer, seaward margin of a coral reef, also referring to the seaward side of a barrier reef or atoll.

A shallow (less than a depth of 200 m), sheltered body of water separated from the open sea by coral reefs; also refers to the area between the shore and a fringing reef, between the coast and a barrier reef, or the portion of an atoll surrounded by the reef.
Area between reefs typically consisting of sandy substrate (see 9.4), but sometimes also with clay or silt sediments (see 9.5 and 9.6).
Area between reefs consisting predominantly of coral or calcareous fragments.

level1.name: Seagrass (submerged)
level1.examples: A bottom habitat consisting predominantly of grass-like marine flowering plants that grow and reproduce while submerged in seawater, such as eelgrass and turtle grass.

level1.name: Estuaries
level1.examples: semi-enclosed coastal embayment where fresh water and seawater meet and mix.

habitats.name: Marine - Oceanic
habitats.examples: The pelagic habitat deeper than and beyond the continental or island shelf (see 9.0 and 9.1).

level1.name: Epipelagic (0–200 m)
level1.examples: The oceanic pelagic environment from the surface to a depth of around 200 m; also refers to the lighted or photic pelagic zone.

level1.name: Mesopelagic (200–1,000
level1.examples: Uppermost oceanic pelagic aphotic zone from a depth of approximately 200 to 1,000 m.

level1.name: Bathypelagic (1,000–4,000 m)
level1.examples: Pelagic aphotic zone lying between the mesopelagic and abyssalpelagic zones between 1,000 to 4,000 m.

level1.name: Abyssopelagic (4,000–6,000 m)
level1.examples: Pelagic aphotic zone from a depth of 4,000 to 6,000 m.

habitats.name: Marine - Deep Ocean Floor (Benthic and Demersal)
habitats.examples: The bottom habitats described in the marine deep ocean floor zone are used by both benthic (living on or in the substrate at the bottom) and demersal (typically free-swimming near the bottom) organisms.

level1.name: Continental Slope/Bathyl zone (200–4,000 m)
level1.examples: The bottom habitat on the steeper, seaward section of the continental or island margin from a depth of around 200 to 2,000 m.

level2.name: Hard Substrate
level2.examples: Bottom type consisting of loose or consolidated rock, including deep karst systems (see 9.2 and 9.3).

level2.name: Soft Substrate
level2.examples: Bottom type consisting of mud or sand or a mixture of mud and sand; most typically consisting of mud (see 9.4, 9.5, 9.6 for sediment sizes).

level1.name: Abyssal Plain (4,000–6,000 m)
level1.examples: The nearly flat area of the deep ocean floor lying between 4,000 and 6,000 m.

level1.name: Abyssal Mountain/Hills (4,000–6,000m)
level1.examples: The hilly or mountainous area of the deep ocean floor lying between 4,000 and 6,000 m.

level1.name: Hadal/Deep Sea Trench (>6000m)
level1.examples: The bottom below 6,000 m.

level1.name: Seamount
level1.examples: Extinct volcano or steep-sided formation that rises abruptly from the deep sea floor but does not reach the surface.

level1.name: Deep Sea Vents (Rifts/Seeps)
level1.examples: An environment with ambient temperatures above normal, on the deep sea floor that depends on geothermal energy as the basis for biological productivity.

habitats.name: Marine - Intertidal
habitats.examples: Area of the shore between the extremes of high and low tides.

level1.name: Rocky Shoreline
level1.examples:
Intertidal shore composed predominantly of consolidated rock or
boulders (see 9.2).

level1.name: Sandy Shorelines and/or Beaches, Sand Bars, Spits, etc.
level1.examples: Intertidal shore composed predominantly of sandy sediments (see 9.4 for sediment size characteristics).

level1.name: Shingle and/or Pebble Shoreline and/or Beaches
level1.examples: Intertidal shore composed predominantly of pebble and cobble sediments (see 9.3 for sediment size characteristics).

level1.name: Mud Shoreline and Intertidal Mud Flats
level1.examples: Intertidal shore or bottom composed predominantly of mud or sandy-mud sediments (see 9.4 and 9.5 for sediment size characteristics).

level1.name: Salt Marshes (Emergent Grasses)
level1.examples: A grassy area that extends along the shores of estuaries and sheltered coasts in temperate and subpolar regions with emergent vegetation rooted in soils alternately inundated and drained by tidal action.

level1.name: Tidepools
level1.examples: An intertidal depression in rocks or in sandy beaches that continues to hold water during low tide (also called tidal pools).

level1.name: Mangrove Submerged Roots
level1.examples: Intertidal zone in mangrove forests (see 1.7).

habitats.name: Marine - Coastal/Supratidal
habitats.examples: Coastal habitats above the high tide mark

level1.name: Sea Cliffs and Rocky Offshore Islands
level1.examples: include limestone areas. Further to be defined

level1.name: Coastal Caves/Karst
level1.examples: Karsts, sea caves and other subterranean hydrological systems along the coast. (See 9.2 and 12.1).

level1.name: Coastal Sand Dunes
level1.examples: Dune systems (including humid dune slacks).

level1.name: Coastal Brackish/Saline Lagoons/Marine Lakes
level1.examples: Brackish to saline lagoons and lakes with at least one relatively narrow connection to the sea. Often formed from sea inlets by silting and cut off from the sea by sand or mud banks.

level1.name: Coastal Freshwater Lakes
level1.examples: Includes freshwater delta lagoons (see 5.5 and 5.6).

level1.name: Arable Land
level1.examples: Includes cereal fields, rice paddies, perennial crops, orchards and groves (but see 14.3 and 14.4).

level1.name: Pastureland
level1.examples: Includes fertilized or re-seeded permanent grasslands, sometimes treated with selective herbicides, with very impoverished flora and fauna. Also includes secondary grasslands and wooded farmland.

level1.name: Plantations
level1.examples:
A plantation is an intentional planting of a crop, on a larger scale, usually for uses other than cereal production or pasture. The term is currently most often used for plantings of trees and shrubs. The term tends also to be used for plantings maintained on economic bases other than that of subsistence farming. Plantations are typically (but not exclusively) found in tropical or semitropical countries and usually require resident labourers.
Examples include cotton, tobacco, sugar cane, banana, sisal, coffee, rubber, oil palm, coconut, timber trees, pineapples.

level1.name: Rural Gardens
level1.examples: Rural gardens are located in a rural setting, serving families whose main income comes from wage labour (rural or urban). Rural gardens differ from arable land production by the following features which are usually, but by no means in all cases, found simultaneously: (1) cropping plants for personal consumption that cannot be collected nor supplied by arable farming, (2) small plots, (3) proximity to the house, (4) fencing, (5) mixed or dense planting of a great number of annual, semi-permanent, and perennial crops, (6) a high intensity of land use, (7) land cultivation several times a year, (8) permanence of cultivation, and (9) cultivation with hand implements. These gardens also provide space and/or fodder for the raising of small animals (usually poultry, rodents and small ruminants). In extreme cases, the rural garden may be the only source of livelihood and income for the rural poor. If enough space is available, small cash crops may be produced and exchanged or sold for purchased food.

level1.name: Urban Areas
level1.examples: Occurs throughout the world. Usually metropolitan and commercial areas dominated by asphalt, concrete and roof. Includes buildings, lawns and parks.

level1.name: Subtropical/Tropical Heavily degraded Former Forest
level1.examples: Former subtropical or tropical forest that has been extensively cleared or impacted by human activities. Often there is some degree of regeneration or there are small fragments of forest remaining.

level1.name: Water Storage Areas
level1.examples: Generally over 8 ha. Includes reservoirs, barrages, dams and impoundments.

level1.name: Ponds
level1.examples: Generally below 8 ha. Includes farm ponds, stock ponds, small tanks.

level1.name: Aquaculture Ponds
level1.examples: For example, fish or shrimp ponds.

level1.name: Salt Exploitation Sites
level1.examples: Salt pans, salines, etc.

level1.name: Excavations (open)
level1.examples: Gravel, brick, clay pits, borrow pits and mining pools.

level1.name: Wastewater Treatment Areas
level1.examples: Sewage farms, settling ponds, oxidation basins, etc.

level1.name: Irrigated Land
level1.examples: Includes irrigation channels and paddy (rice) fields.

level1.name: Seasonally Flooded Agricultural Land
level1.examples: Including intensively managed or grazed wet meadow or pasture.

level1.name: Canals and Drainage Channels, Ditches
level1.examples: Linear excavations (varying enormously in size) made specifically to improve drainage of farmland, for controlling river courses, for controlling flow of water, for allowing ship movement, etc.

level1.name: Karst and Other Subterrranean Hydrological Systems
level1.examples: Human-made subterranean systems.

level1.name: Marine Anthropogenic Structures
level1.examples: Artificial reefs, docks, seawalls, rip rap, etc.

level1.name: Mariculture Cages
level1.examples: Cages (made out of net or mesh) located in an open environment which includes both the sea and inland brackish water areas, for the culture of organisms, both plants and animals.

level1.name: Mari/Brackish-culture Ponds
level1.examples: Human-made saltwater or brackish ponds for the cultivation of organisms, both plants and animals.

habitats.name: Introduced Vegetation
habitats.examples:
Includes only non-cultivated species or those that have escaped from
cultivation.

habitats.name: Other
habitats.examples: A habitat type not covered by any of the other categories in the No type specified system.
